title: The Meaning Audit
subtitle: Does your brand give people a reason to care before they read a single feature?

persona_selector.text: Where is your brand right now?

answers.label: Idea stage, brand not built yet

questions.text: Before you list a single feature, does your brand give someone a reason to care?
Can a stranger tell what you believe or stand for, not just what you sell?
When people encounter your brand, do they feel something before they evaluate anything?

low.headline: You're answering 'what' before anyone asked 'why care'
low.text: Right now your brand leads with what the product does, but people decide what something says about them before they care what it does. A MacBook outsells a faster, cheaper PC because it means something. Lead with features and you've quietly agreed to compete on price.
steps: Write the one thing your brand believes, before any feature, and put it first
Replace your lead message from 'what it does' to 'why it matters to who you're for'
Make sure the first thing someone feels is a point of view, not a spec sheet

mid.headline: The meaning is there, the features keep crowding it out
mid.text: You have a real reason to care, but features keep elbowing to the front and diluting it. Meaning is the part people pay extra for, and the part most brands bury under capabilities.
steps: Audit your homepage and deck for where features jump ahead of meaning and reorder them
Lead every key surface with the belief, then let features prove it
Cut feature lists in half wherever the meaning can carry the weight

high.headline: You lead with meaning, and it shows
high.text: People get a reason to care before they hit a feature, which is exactly why a brand earns a premium instead of a price war. The work now is deepening the belief and making it unmistakably yours.
steps: Sharpen your point of view until no competitor could credibly claim it
Let features serve as proof of the belief, never the headline
Protect the meaning-first order as you add products and pages

questions.text: Does your brand hold an actual stance, something it's for and against?
Could your brand 'have opinions' the way Oatly does, or is it just describing a category?
Would the right customer feel 'this is for me' and the wrong one feel 'this isn't'?

answers.label: No, we try to appeal to everyone
Sharply, it clearly picks its people

low.headline: Your brand is describing a category, not holding a view
low.text: Oatly didn't win the fridge with oat-to-liquid ratios, they won by making a carton feel like a point of view. A brand with no stance is forgettable and interchangeable. Trying to be for everyone is how you become meaningful to no one.
steps: Decide what your brand is genuinely for and against, and say it out loud
Give the brand a voice with an actual opinion, not neutral category language
Accept that the right stance will repel some people, that's the point

mid.headline: There's a view in there, it's just too polite
mid.text: Your brand has the beginnings of a stance but keeps softening it to avoid alienating anyone. The softening is exactly what makes it forgettable. Meaning comes from conviction, not consensus.
steps: Take your softest brand statement and rewrite it with real conviction
Find the belief your ideal customer shares and lean into it hard
Let the brand sort people, the ones it repels were never yours

high.headline: Your brand has a worldview
high.text: You hold a stance, sort your people, and have a voice with opinions, which is what makes a brand impossible to mistake for anyone else. The leverage now is consistency and courage, keeping the view sharp everywhere.
steps: Make sure the stance shows up in every surface, not just the manifesto
Keep the edges sharp, don't sand them down as you grow
Use the clarity of your view to attract people competitors can't

questions.text: When you win, is it on meaning and fit, or mostly on price and spec comparisons?
If you swapped your logo for a competitor's, would anyone notice a difference in what you stand for?
How often do you feel pressure to discount to close?

answers.label: Almost never, meaning holds the price

low.headline: Feature-first messaging is quietly costing you margin
low.text: When a brand only describes the product, the only lever left is price. That's the feature-first tax: you compete on spec, you discount to close, and you train customers to shop you against cheaper alternatives. Meaning is what lets a brand hold its price.
steps: Find where you're competing on spec and reframe around what the choice says about the buyer
Build one message that a competitor couldn't paste their logo onto
Stop leading sales conversations with features, lead with the belief and the fit

mid.headline: You're half on meaning, half on price
mid.text: Sometimes you win on fit, sometimes you slide back into spec comparisons and discounts. Every time you compete on features you invite a cheaper option into the room.
steps: Track your last ten deals: which were won on meaning vs price, and why
Rebuild the price-led ones around what the brand stands for
Give sales a meaning-first opener so they stop leading with specs

high.headline: You win on meaning, not price
high.text: You rarely compete on spec, you're not interchangeable, and you feel little discount pressure, which is what a brand with real meaning earns. Protect it: the pull toward feature-comparison never fully goes away.
steps: Keep messaging anchored on meaning even when a prospect asks to compare specs
Reinforce what makes you un-swappable in every touchpoint
Use your pricing power to invest back into the brand, not into discounts

questions.text: Does using or wearing your brand say something about the customer, the way a MacBook does?

answers.label: Yes, it's part of their identity

questions.text: Do your customers feel like part of something, not just buyers of a product?
Would a customer proudly show your brand to others, unprompted?

answers.label: Yes, they advocate on their own

low.headline: Your brand is a purchase, not a badge
low.text: People pay a premium for what a brand says about them. Right now yours is functional, a thing people buy, not a thing they belong to. Give people something to belong to and they'll choose you over cheaper, even better-specced options.
steps: Define what someone is saying about themselves when they choose you
Build the brand so using it signals identity, not just utility
Create a reason for customers to feel part of something, not just a transaction

mid.headline: Belonging is starting, it's not yet a badge
mid.text: Some customers feel a connection, but it's not strong enough that they'd show you off unprompted. The gap between 'satisfied buyer' and 'proud member' is where premium and word-of-mouth live.
steps: Find your most loyal customers and articulate what belonging to your brand means to them
Make that identity visible and shareable in the product and brand
Give people something to advocate for, not just a product to use

high.headline: People belong to your brand
high.text: Customers wear you as a badge, feel part of something, and advocate unprompted, which is the strongest position a brand can hold. Keep feeding the belonging as you scale so it doesn't thin out.
steps: Protect what the community values as you grow, don't dilute it for reach
Keep giving members new ways to signal they belong
Let advocates shape the brand, they're your most credible voice

questions.text: Is your brand's voice and look consistent everywhere, or does it change surface to surface?
Is the thing that makes you recognizable deliberate, or accidental?
Do you win on intentionality (small, deliberate moves) rather than big spend?

answers.label: No, we assume it takes big budget
Yes, intent beats budget for us

low.headline: Your recognizability is accidental, and it's leaking
low.text: Oatly spent almost nothing on the thing that makes them unmistakable, it's just the most deliberate part of the company. One consistent voice everywhere beats one big campaign. If your brand changes surface to surface, you're paying for reach you then throw away.
steps: Pin down the two or three deliberate moves that make you recognizable and apply them everywhere
Make consistency the budget: one voice on every surface beats one expensive push
Treat intentionality, not spend, as your competitive edge

mid.headline: Consistent in places, drifting in others
mid.text: Your brand holds together on the main surfaces but drifts on the edges, and the drift is where recognizability leaks. Small, deliberate consistency compounds; inconsistency quietly resets it.
steps: Find the surfaces where the brand drifts and bring them back in line
Document the few deliberate moves that make you you, so nothing dilutes them
Choose deliberate consistency over occasional big splashes

high.headline: Deliberate and unmistakable
high.text: Your brand is consistent everywhere and the recognizability is intentional, which is exactly how small brands out-punch big budgets. Keep defending it, consistency is the first thing that erodes under growth and new hands.
steps: Codify the deliberate moves so new work stays unmistakably yours
Review every new surface against the system before it ships
Keep betting on intentionality over spend, it's your edge

cta.headline: Turn this score into a brand people belong to
cta.description: You can see where your brand is describing instead of meaning something. The next step is making meaning systematic, so every post, page, and product says one thing people want to belong to. Book a 30-minute call and I'll show you where to start and what to fix first.
